While massive ETFs like Motilal Oswal Nasdaq 100 (MON100) have over ₹13,000 Crores in assets, the Nasdaq Q50 ETF (MONQ50) held less than ₹200 Crores. Because the float was minuscule and zero new units could be minted, speculative capital easily cornered the order book, triggering artificial upper circuits with modest volumes.
MONQ50 was the most extreme casualty, but it was not alone. Mirae Asset NYSE FANG+ ETF (MAFANG) traded at a 65% premium (₹276 price vs ₹180 NAV). Motilal Oswal Nasdaq 100 traded at 15% to 30% premiums. Uninformed investors across India were systematically overpaying for US tech exposure.
Investing in an ETF at an inflated price is mathematically guaranteed to generate negative alpha. When the premium collapses back to NAV, investors lose money even if the underlying index rises. Sovereign investors must check live iNAV, avoid frozen creation funds, and execute direct overseas remittances when domestic pipes are blocked.

When you buy an ETF at a 50% or 300% premium, you are paying real money for nothing. You are paying ₹400 for a basket of stocks that the fund house can only liquidate for ₹100.
 If an AMC announces that creation of new units is suspended (due to regulatory limits or capital controls), the ETF ceases to behave like an index fund. It becomes an illiquid closed-end token susceptible to manipulation.
Avoid international ETFs with an Asset Under Management (AUM) below ₹500 Crores. A tiny pool like MONQ50 (under ₹200 Crores) can be cornered and pushed into upper circuits with as little as ₹10 to ₹15 Crores of speculative volume.
Always use strict limit orders anchored to the published iNAV. Never buy at the offer price if the ask spread is blowing out.
A diversified index ETF cannot fundamentally double in five days while its underlying index is flat. Any rapid upward price surge without an underlying NAV surge is an artificial trap.

Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) are not simple mutual funds; they are exchange-traded securities whose prices depend on continuous market arbitrage. When the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) froze overseas investment limits at $7 Billion, Authorized Participants could no longer create new units to meet surging investor demand. Combined with a SEBI price-band rule change that ratcheted upper circuits daily, the Motilal Oswal Nasdaq Q50 ETF (MONQ50) exploded by over 250% to ₹471. It traded at an insane 300% premium above its actual net asset value (NAV) of ~₹115. Once speculative momentum dried up, the fund crashed 46% in two trading sessions, wiping out uninformed retail buyers who bought a 100-rupee note for 400 rupees.
